candidato.titulo: Experimental GLS-1 inhibitor demonstrates antitumor activity in advanced treatment-resistant ovarian cancer
candidato.resumo: Combining the experimental therapy IACS-6274 with targeted therapy bevacizumab and paclitaxel chemotherapy showed promising antitumor activity in a Phase I trial of patients with advanced platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, according to new results presented by researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

texto_fonte:
Experimental GLS-1 inhibitor demonstrates antitumor activity in advanced treatment-resistant ovarian cancer
Combining the experimental therapy IACS-6274 with targeted therapy bevacizumab and paclitaxel chemotherapy showed promising antitumor activity in a Phase I trial of patients with advanced platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, according to new results presented by researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
IACS-6274 is a targeted therapy developed by UT MD Anderson's Therapeutics Discovery division that is designed to block a key metabolic enzyme. The data were presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics by Principal Investigator Timothy Yap, M.B.B.S., Ph.D., professor of Investigational Cancer Therapeutics and head of clinical development in UT MD Anderson's Therapeutics Discovery division.
"We saw deep and durable responses in these patients with advanced, hard-to-treat ovarian cancer," Yap said. "In 10 patients who either had a partial response or had stable disease, the responses lasted at least four months, with some lasting nearly three years. This is a meaningful difference for these patients, who currently do not have any good options once their disease reaches this stage."
What were the key results of the IACS-6274 trial?
The trial included 14 patients, including 13 patients whose ovarian cancers did not respond to platinum-based therapies. All patients' tumors had stopped responding to standard-of-care treatment.
Of the 13 patients evaluable for efficacy, nine had confirmed partial responses, with their tumors shrinking by at least 30%. Three patients had stable disease, meaning their cancers neither grew nor shrank. Eleven of the 13 patients had disease control 12 weeks after the start of the trial.
The therapy was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities. Adverse effects were mostly mild nausea, fatigue, hair loss, anemia, nosebleeds, elevated liver enzymes, neutropenia and nail and vision disturbances. More severe side effects included higher-grade neutropenia, elevated blood pressure and anemia, but they were successfully treated.
How does IACS-6274 work?
About a quarter of all ovarian cancers are initially resistant to platinum-based chemotherapy, and an even larger number eventually develop resistance to the treatment. For either set of patients, the standard of care is a combination of the chemotherapy paclitaxel and the VEGF inhibitor bevacizumab.
Most cancers will develop resistance to this combination within a year by becoming overly dependent on a nutrient called glutamine. Scientists have theorized that inhibiting glutamine could overcome resistance, but broad inhibition in previous trials resulted in dose-limiting side effects.
IACS-6274 was developed to inhibit glutaminase-1 (GLS-1), which can block the ability of these cancers to access glutamine. Importantly, it does so without affecting glutaminase-2, an important enzyme in several biological processes. That selectivity is where many previous attempts at GLS inhibition failed.
Additionally, IACS-6274 was designed to be better absorbed than previous GLS inhibitors. Modern genetic testing has also uncovered a subset of cancers that lack an enzyme called ASNS, which means they are completely dependent on glutamine for survival and are more likely to benefit from this treatment. Eight of the 14 patients on this trial had ASNS loss, with six of them being partial responders.
What's next for IACS-6274?
Based on these data, 15 additional patients will be treated with the combination on the trial, with further expansion planned with an additional 15 patients if the results continue to be positive.
"This is really an exciting trial for us because it's a perfect example of our ability to develop a therapy that addresses a need we see in the clinic," said Tim Heffernan, Ph.D., vice president and head of research and development in UT MD Anderson's Therapeutics Discovery Division. "It's also an example of how the trial data feed back into our research to continue to better select patients who could benefit from this therapy."

candidato.titulo: Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
candidato.resumo: Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.

texto_fonte:
Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.
Now, researchers at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center—Centro Nacional de Supercomputación (BSC-CNS) have developed ContextMirror2.0, a tool capable of identifying relationships between proteins by using the information that millions of years of evolution left behind in their amino acid sequences.
The study, published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology, reveals how the algorithm compares the evolution of thousands of proteins across different species and searches for pairs exhibiting related evolutionary patterns. Thus, if two proteins evolved together (coevolved) and display correlated changes in their sequences, researchers can deduce that they interact and likely share related functions.
By applying this system across the entire protein set of three bacterial species (Escherichia coli, Salmonella enterica and Staphylococcus aureus), the researchers validated the method by recovering previously known associations while also identifying interaction patterns specific to each of the three species.
"ContextMirror2.0 reliably predicts hundreds of protein interactions in E. coli and identifies which ones are species-specific, a distinction that generic AI methods do not make and that could help uncover new targeted therapeutic targets," explained Alfonso Valencia, study lead and director of the Life Sciences Department at BSC.
One of the key differences between this tool and other methods for predicting protein interactions is that it does not require training on examples of known interactions. This avoids the biases that can arise with artificial intelligence, which tends to be trained on heavily studied organisms or proteins.
As a result, it serves as an especially valuable complementary tool for analyzing poorly characterized species where little prior experimental evidence exists.
"If you are going to study a bacterium about which nothing is known, you can use this algorithm to get a broad picture of its interaction network, as it narrows millions of combinations down to a small set of candidate proteins with a high probability of interacting, streamlining experimental work in the lab," explained Miguel Fernández, BSC researcher and first author of the study.
Eighteen years later, the project marks the culmination of ContextMirror, a study published by Valencia in 2008 that laid the groundwork for the current methodology but could only be applied to small sets of proteins due to the limitations of the era, including scarce data in bacterial genomic databases and limited computational analysis capacity.
A 'step zero' for biology and health care
To tackle the roughly 9 million protein pairs in E. coli, the team turned to the supercomputing power of MareNostrum 4 and later MareNostrum 5, selecting the 1,000 highest-scoring pairs identified by the algorithm. Of these 1,000 interactions, 400 had prior validation, while the remaining 600 represented plausible associations never before described.
"Predicting all protein interactions within a complete organism remains a highly complex challenge in modern biology. With this tool, we offer an ideal 'step zero' so the scientific community can place unknown proteins within their functional contexts and target their experimental trials much more precisely," noted Fernández.
To ensure the tool is useful to everyone, alongside the version optimized for supercomputing, the team also developed and released a lightweight, open-source library of ContextMirror2.0. This allows researchers to analyze smaller sets of proteins on a personal computer in an accessible way without requiring major computing infrastructure.
Looking ahead, the authors conclude, this tool and its comparative approach could facilitate the identification of therapeutic targets and the study of critical mechanisms such as bacterial antibiotic resistance in modern medicine.
Publication details
Miguel Fernandez-Martin et al., Sequence-based coevolutionary prediction of species-specific interactomes, PLOS Computational Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014839

candidato.titulo: What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges
candidato.resumo: The engineering challenges of industrial drone autonomy include GNSS reliability, SLAM, sensor fusion, obstacle avoidance, and UAV validation. The post What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
An autonomous drone can complete a carefully planned inspection route in a controlled environment and still struggle with the same route at an operating industrial facility. A steel structure may obstruct satellite signals, reflective equipment may distort depth measurements, and a wind gust may push the aircraft outside its planned trajectory. Each disturbance can be manageable in isolation. The difficulty emerges when several occur simultaneously.
This exposes a fundamental challenge in industrial drone autonomy: performance depends on interactions between subsystems whose assumptions are rarely independent.
A navigation algorithm may estimate position accurately under favorable sensing conditions. An obstacle detector may identify nearby structures during controlled testing. A flight controller may maintain stable tracking under a nominal payload. None of these results independently establishes that the integrated system can safely complete an inspection near energized infrastructure, confined structures, or operating machinery.
Reliable deployment requires engineers to understand how uncertainty propagates through localization, perception, planning, control, and inspection-data acquisition. It also requires evidence that the system can recognize when its estimates are no longer trustworthy.
Why industrial environments challenge autonomous navigation
Industrial facilities introduce environmental conditions that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory demonstrations.
Metallic surfaces, repetitive structural patterns, narrow access corridors, moving equipment, airborne particulates, and changing illumination can affect multiple sensors simultaneously. These conditions create both geometric constraints and uncertainty in the information available to the autonomy system.
Consider a hypothetical UAV inspecting pipework beside a steel-framed processing facility.
As the aircraft approaches the structure, GNSS measurements become less reliable. Repetitive pipes complicate visual feature matching, while reflective surfaces produce inconsistent depth observations. Meanwhile, the flight controller must reject aerodynamic disturbances caused by nearby structures.
The resulting problem is not simply inaccurate positioning. The autonomy stack must decide whether its remaining localization confidence supports continued flight, whether detected free space is sufficiently reliable, and whether the planned maneuver remains dynamically feasible.
These decisions are coupled. A localization error can corrupt obstacle coordinates, while a delayed perception update can cause the planner to act on geometry that no longer represents the aircraft’s surroundings.
The practical engineering objective is therefore not uninterrupted autonomous operation under every condition. It is predictable behavior within a defined operational envelope, including when that envelope is exceeded.
GNSS limitations and the localization problem
Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning provides an important absolute reference for outdoor autonomous UAV navigation. However, industrial structures introduce several failure mechanisms.
Buildings, tanks, and overhead equipment can block direct satellite signals. Reflections from metallic surfaces create multipath interference, causing a receiver to process signals that have traveled indirect paths.
Real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning can improve accuracy by using carrier-phase measurements and correction data. However, RTK does not eliminate obstruction, multipath, cycle slips, or poor satellite geometry. A fixed ambiguity solution should not be treated as an unconditional guarantee of accurate positioning.
Combining absolute and relative localization
An inertial measurement unit (IMU) estimates angular velocity and specific force. Integrated inertial measurements support high-frequency motion propagation, but bias and noise cause errors to accumulate over time.
Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera observations with inertial measurements to estimate relative motion. Published work such as VINS-Mono demonstrates nonlinear optimization approaches that integrate visual and inertial constraints for state estimation.
Lidar-based odometry provides another approach, using geometric correspondence between successive scans. LIO-SAM, for example, combines lidar and inertial measurements in a factor-graph framework with mapping and loop-closure capabilities.
These approaches have different weaknesses. Visual methods depend on illumination, image quality, and observable features. Lidar methods can struggle with insufficient geometric constraints, adverse returns, or sensor-specific limitations.
Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) additionally maintains a representation of the environment while estimating the robot’s pose. Loop closure can correct accumulated trajectory drift when a previously visited location is recognized, although incorrect associations can introduce significant map errors.
For industrial UAVs, engineers must also distinguish local consistency from global accuracy. A drone may maintain a stable relative trajectory while its estimated position gradually diverges from the facility’s surveyed coordinate system.
This distinction becomes critical when an inspection requires repeatable measurements at known asset locations.
Obstacle avoidance is more than detecting objects
Obstacle avoidance is often described as a perception problem. In operational UAV systems, it is an end-to-end timing and control problem.
A typical pipeline must acquire sensor measurements, estimate obstacle geometry, update the local environment representation, generate a collision-free trajectory, and issue commands that the aircraft can physically execute.
Each stage introduces latency and uncertainty.
Sensor limitations affect the available flight envelope
Lidar provides active range measurements and can support geometric mapping under varying visible-light conditions. However, transparent materials, highly reflective surfaces, thin wires, and unfavorable incidence angles can produce missing or misleading returns.
Stereo vision estimates depth from image correspondence. Its performance depends on camera geometry, texture, illumination, and disparity estimation. Depth uncertainty generally increases with distance for a fixed stereo baseline and disparity uncertainty.
Active depth cameras introduce their own range, illumination, interference, and surface-response constraints.
No single sensing modality provides reliable coverage of every industrial obstacle. A practical design must account for sensor field of view, blind regions, minimum detection range, and the possibility that a hazard remains unobserved.
Planning latency becomes physical distance
For a simplified one-dimensional braking model, the distance required to respond to an obstacle can be approximated as:
d_required ≈ vT + v²/(2a)
Here, v is the aircraft’s speed toward the obstacle, T is the combined detection-to-control delay, and a is the achievable deceleration magnitude.
This model assumes constant speed during the delay and constant deceleration afterward. It excludes additional clearance margins, uncertainty, wind, and complex multi-axis flight dynamics.
Nevertheless, it illustrates why latency matters. Doubling flight speed doubles the distance traveled during processing delay and quadruples the idealized braking-distance term.
A collision-avoidance system must therefore be evaluated against the aircraft’s actual maneuvering capability, not simply its obstacle detection range.
Dynamic obstacles add another complication. A path considered clear at the beginning of a planning cycle may no longer be safe when the corresponding control command is executed.
Sensor fusion and state estimation under real-world conditions
Sensor fusion improves navigation by combining measurements with complementary characteristics. It also introduces dependencies that must be explicitly managed.
An extended Kalman filter (EKF), commonly used for state estimation, propagates the system state through a motion model and corrects that prediction using sensor observations.
The measurement update depends on the estimated uncertainty of both the prediction and the observations. If those uncertainty models are inaccurate, the filter may become overconfident.
For example, GNSS measurements affected by multipath may exhibit correlated errors that are poorly represented by a simple independent-noise assumption. Accepting such measurements with excessive confidence can pull the state estimate away from the true trajectory.
Innovation residuals and normalized innovation squared tests can help identify inconsistent measurements. However, statistical gating depends on appropriate noise models and does not guarantee detection of every failure.
Calibration and synchronization are part of navigation
A camera and IMU must have accurately characterized spatial transformations and timing relationships.
Even a small temporal offset can create systematic visual-inertial estimation errors during rapid rotation. Incorrect extrinsic calibration can similarly produce inconsistent motion estimates.
The Kalibr calibration framework provides established methods for estimating camera-IMU spatial and temporal relationships.
Engineers should also monitor estimator consistency, covariance behavior, measurement rejection rates, and the duration for which the system can operate without reliable absolute position updates.
A crucial distinction is that estimator covariance represents uncertainty under the assumed model. It is not necessarily a complete measure of actual error when the model itself is wrong.
Environmental disturbances and flight control reliability
Autonomous navigation cannot be separated from the aircraft’s flight dynamics.
Wind gusts introduce external forces and moments that disturb trajectory tracking. Near buildings, airflow can become spatially variable, producing disturbances that differ from those encountered in unobstructed flight. For additional operational context, an overview of drone wind resistance levels provides a practical explanation of wind ratings and operating constraints; those ratings still require interpretation against aircraft configuration and site conditions.
Payload changes affect mass, center of gravity, inertia, and power requirements. Vibration can degrade IMU measurements and camera image quality, particularly when mechanical isolation and filtering are insufficient.
Actuator saturation creates another important limitation. A controller may calculate a corrective command that the motors cannot deliver because of thrust limits, battery voltage, or competing attitude-control demands.
Control-loop stability must therefore be evaluated across expected payload configurations and operating conditions.
Embedded computing introduces competing constraints
Autonomous UAVs often execute localization, perception, mapping, planning, communications, and mission management on limited onboard computing resources.
Higher-resolution sensing may improve geometric detail but increase processing load, memory use, power consumption, and latency.
A computationally intensive SLAM update can also compete with perception or planning workloads.
Engineers need to characterize worst-case execution times, deadline misses, scheduling behavior, and degraded-operation strategies rather than relying solely on average processor utilization.
A navigation system that produces accurate estimates too late for the controller to use them is not operationally reliable.
Why autonomous inspection data can still be unreliable
Successfully navigating an inspection route does not guarantee that the resulting measurements are suitable for engineering decisions.
Navigation accuracy and inspection-data accuracy are related but distinct.
A UAV may maintain a stable position while capturing blurred imagery, poorly calibrated thermal measurements, or insufficiently overlapping photographs.
For photogrammetric inspection, reconstruction quality depends on camera calibration, image geometry, surface texture, exposure, and the distribution of viewing angles. High image overlap alone cannot compensate for weak geometry or systematic calibration errors.
Georeferencing adds further dependencies, including coordinate transformations, surveyed control, camera-to-body alignment, and synchronization between position estimates and image capture.
Thermal imaging introduces different limitations. Apparent temperature depends on emissivity, reflected radiation, viewing geometry, atmospheric conditions, and instrument calibration. A thermal anomaly should not automatically be interpreted as a confirmed equipment defect.
Lidar inspection similarly depends on scan geometry, range noise, incidence angle, point density, and motion compensation.
For repeat inspections, engineers should evaluate whether the same physical feature can be measured consistently across missions.
That requires separating repeatability from absolute accuracy and recording sufficient metadata to identify changes in sensing conditions. An inspection workflow should therefore validate both the flight trajectory and the quality of the collected engineering evidence.
Human oversight, failure recovery, and operational safety
Autonomous operation does not remove the need for supervisory control.
A robust system should define the conditions under which it can continue, pause, return, land, or transfer authority to a human operator.
These decisions require explicit fault-handling logic.
Loss of GNSS alone may not justify terminating a mission if alternative localization remains sufficiently reliable. However, simultaneous localization degradation and restricted maneuvering space may make continued autonomous flight unacceptable.
Return-to-home behavior also has limitations. It depends on available localization, a suitable return path, obstacle clearance, and sufficient energy.
In a GNSS-denied or structurally confined environment, returning along a predefined route may be less appropriate than executing a separately validated contingency maneuver.
Lost-link procedures should distinguish temporary communication interruption from broader navigation or control failures.
Human intervention remains meaningful only when operators have adequate situational awareness, clear authority, and enough time to respond.
For U.S. operations, engineering procedures must also align with applicable FAA requirements and authorizations. Autonomous mission execution does not independently remove regulatory responsibilities.
The relevant safety question is not whether a UAV can fly without continuous manual input. It is whether the combined autonomous and supervisory system behaves acceptably when assumptions fail.
How engineers should validate autonomous drone deployments
Industrial deployment readiness cannot be established through a single successful demonstration.
Testing should combine simulation, hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, controlled flight trials, and progressively representative operating environments.
Simulation allows engineers to reproduce faults and explore scenarios that may be unsafe to introduce during early flight testing. However, simulated sensor models, aerodynamic disturbances, and environmental geometry cannot capture every physical effect.
Field validation is needed to establish whether the assumptions used in simulation remain credible.
Define measurable acceptance criteria
A practical validation program should include metrics that connect algorithm behavior to operational outcomes.
These metrics require careful definitions.
Localization error should be evaluated against an independent reference where feasible, rather than against the estimator’s own reported trajectory. Root-mean-square error alone may conceal short-duration excursions that are critical near obstacles.
Obstacle detection performance should distinguish false positives from missed detections and account for obstacle size, material, distance, and approach geometry.
Mission completion rates should report the tested scenario distribution and failure definitions. A high completion rate in benign conditions provides limited evidence about operation near industrial structures.
Intervention frequency is useful only when the criteria for intervention and the level of autonomy are consistent.
Test interactions between failures
Individual fault tests are necessary but insufficient.
A more revealing scenario might combine intermittent GNSS, reduced visual texture, increased processing latency, and moderate wind disturbances.
The purpose is not to demonstrate that the UAV can tolerate every conceivable combination. It is to identify the boundaries within which the system remains controllable and capable of making trustworthy decisions.
Engineers should document these boundaries as operational constraints, including conditions that trigger mission suspension or recovery.
Reliable autonomy is a system-level property
Industrial drone deployments expose the limitations of evaluating autonomy through isolated subsystem performance.
Accurate localization does not guarantee safe obstacle avoidance. Successful obstacle avoidance does not guarantee stable flight control. Stable flight does not guarantee useful inspection measurements. And successful mission execution does not demonstrate that the system will respond appropriately to degraded sensing or unexpected faults.
Reliable autonomy emerges when sensing, estimation, planning, control, data acquisition, and human supervision are designed and validated together.
For robotics engineers, the central challenge is not merely improving individual algorithms. It is establishing measurable operating boundaries, understanding how errors propagate between subsystems, and ensuring that the aircraft can recognize and respond when its assumptions no longer hold.
That is the difference between demonstrating autonomous flight and engineering an autonomous system suitable for industrial operations.
About the Author
Jonathan Metzelaar is a contributor associated with ZenaDrone Inc., a company working in unmanned aerial systems. His contribution examines technical considerations in autonomous UAV navigation, sensing, and industrial deployment.

candidato.titulo: Presentation: AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production
candidato.resumo: The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost. By Garima Bajpaj, Martin Reynolds, Patrick Debois, Gunnar Grosch, Renato Losio

texto_fonte:
Transcript
Renato Losio: Today we'll discuss how AI is changing software delivery, so from code generation to production, how AI-assisted software delivery is changing in our crazy times.
In this roundtable, we are going to discuss how AI is changing the way organizations are going to build, test, secure, deploy, operate software. What is the real challenge today? We are all familiar with AI in general now and how it's changing every aspect of our developer life, but one of the challenges we discuss maybe less is how is integrating AI into the broader engineering lifecycle while maintaining quality, security, and reliability.
My name is Renato Losio. I'm an editor at InfoQ. I'm joined today by four experts coming from different companies, different sectors, different countries. I'd like to give a chance to each one of them to introduce themselves and share their journey, and why they are part of this panel today.
Patrick Debois: My name is Patrick Debois. I have some history in DevOps and CI/CD. I currently help Tessl with building a software factory for your coding agents.
Martin Reynolds: I'm Field CTO at Harness. I spend most of my time working with our customers on everything that we're talking about today. Everything that's after code, build, test, secure, deploy, operate. Also, I say recently, a few months back, I also now co-host a podcast called ShipTalk. We talk about everything that's going on with AI that's in the news.
Garima Bajpai: I'm Garima Bajpai. I bring 25 years of leadership experience leading software development organizations at an enterprise level. Lately, I'm being more known for my work with AI and how AI would scale when it comes to software development. I'm more interested and intrigued by community-driven initiatives, community-driven InnerSourcing work, as well as hackathons, micro and mega hackathons, which we have been doing.
Gunnar Grosch: I'm Gunnar. I'm a developer advocate at Sinch. I have also spent about 25 years or something in the industry building software, working with developer communities. These days, I build and talk a lot about AI agents in production, and working with Sinch, obviously that means a lot of conversational AI in different ways. I also have a podcast with some friends, called, Yells at Cloud.
Software Delivery in the AI Era
Renato Losio: How is AI already changing software delivery in your organization? We are all familiar with developers using coding assistants. We are familiar with maybe agents in pure development. We hope we are not all just vibe coding, but how is it really already affecting software delivery?
Patrick Debois: We're probably going through these phases that everybody went through. Like you described, first it was your completion, then it was your coding agent. A lot of people still do that with their Claude and their OpenAI working together on their laptop. Then we started seeing, there's a lot of context. We're putting knowledge back somewhere in skills and more information, so the agents become better. We improve the harness. That's all good. I would call that our solo level, team shared level working together. About six or seven months ago, we switched to using a central pipeline, what we call the factory in general, where we're all working more through filing tickets, the agents take care of it, so it's less running on our laptop. That created a different dynamic in the company from the solo dev to actually product, engineering, sales, support, all working together. That's the transformation that we went through. I think that's not unique.
Renato Losio: You mentioned before the entire conversational chat and whatever. What's your take on this?
Gunnar Grosch: I think we're seeing a similar thing that Patrick just described. There are different parts of the development lifecycle that are changing. I think part of it is about trusting it to be able to hand off things. I think we're seeing it in stages. One part that is easy to handle is the research part. Before you start writing code, previously you had to usually do a lot of research, figure out how a codebase worked or how an API worked and so on. Those are things that are easy to hand off, let agents do, and then you get the result back and you can take part of it. Same with the other end of the lifecycle, where you deploy, you test, you iterate, and you have that loop over and over again. Also, fairly easy to hand off to agents and let them take part of it.
What I'm still seeing a lot is that the step in between, that's still where developers or engineers are engaged. They're still doing a lot of the work in that in-between, so handing off the initial work, handing off that last leg of the work, but still doing a lot of the work in between. I think a lot of it comes down to trust, being able to actually hand off that entire work. It's a bit scary.
Agentic Software Delivery, in Prod
Renato Losio: I don't know, really on a personal experience, I can say that if you talk to many practitioners it's, yes, we are experimenting with it. We are doing that. We are doing delivery using agents. When you ask, so are you doing that in production completely and trust, or you did this step? Not yet. Or we have a proof of concept or we have in a small project, but that's a big leap. I think we'll come back often to that.
Martin Reynolds: I think that's something that comes up quite often, especially work with quite a lot of regulated environments, and the trust is a big thing. I think if you had good governance on your delivery process before and you can make sure you can apply it in the same way to agents, then they'd fail the same way a person would fail. The mechanism might not be exactly the same, but I think you need the governance set up the same way, so that they should have things like scoped credentials, policies, approvals, audit trail, so they're not free-roaming agents. Coming back to that gap that was mentioned, it's interesting, because I think you're right. There are things like code review that seems to be an ever-increasing challenge, like test generation, even auto-fix of failed builds and failed deployments, or the ever eternally-growing number of CVEs that seem to exist in the world thanks to AI.
It's like, here's a load more CVEs in your build. All of those things you can use AI to do. You can use it to help you with code review. You can use it to help with test generation. I think it is evolving. One of the fun things about working where I work is that we build a lot of software, and we've been tackling a lot of these problems as we go along.
Garima Bajpai: I actually wanted to add a few things here, because, again, as Patrick and Gunnar alluded to the fact that with AI, the individual productivity has improved. That's a no question that code is no longer the scarce capability. That's a given thing in an enterprise ecosystem. What we see, again, different companies, different communities, different experiences. There are three things which I think are standing out for us. I also come from a critical infrastructure background as well, very controlled and regulated environment. Our testing capabilities, our testing matrices, we see that they are broken now, because we are leading to more next-generation test matrices where the validity for implementing it on a probabilistic LLM application, testing must shift from a statistical threshold to golden data points. LLM-as-judge rubrics comes into play. The second aspect is security. Security must transition to runtime. As DevOps advocates, we have advocated for shift left capabilities, but I think it's also more shift right at this point in time.
The third part, which also from an enterprise perspective, we have been seeing and are struggling with, FinOps, how to adopt token economics at scale. When you work with a 20,000-developer ecosystem, it becomes a very substantial amount of your capability, like how your token economics would shift and how FinOps becomes a very integral part of your ecosystem. These three things I think we have seen that now people are being more conscious about, and we are also seeing governance control levers, guardrails, around our delivery agents to make it more holistic.
Patrick Debois: I love that you're bringing up the compliance, the cost. The way that we started thinking about this is you're building code. Like you said, it's easier. That's fine. Like Martin says, you need to have tests. That is still important. Good engineering practices don't go away. Observabilities that you need, you need the scaling. You need all those pieces in there as well, because what they do is actually they improve the code and they reduce the likelihood of having issues. That's the first piece of you give better context, you write tests, you get less issues. That's one way of dealing with it. The second piece that you see now more and more in people's workflows is a risk analysis. The agent has done all the steps. They added tests. There was an adversarial review. They got a better result. Now it's the fact like, ok, can I actually push this change through?
What is the impact? A simple documentation change is completely different than you touching the authentication piece in your code. People are using ways to look at, ok, should this go directly or not? That is similar to what we did before. A user says this is important, this is not important. This is a risk as well. Then the third piece, very DevOps, like you said, Garima, is when it moves to production, what is the impact? We had the likelihood, the risk, and then the impact. Many people tell me, we don't look at the code anymore. I ask them, ok, what's your application? It's some blog site. It's some random small thing, or it's experimental. candidato.titulo: DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4 times more bandwidth than DDR5 — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
candidato.resumo: Upcoming DDR6 memory cuts module length from 133mm to 74mm while kicking off at 12.8 GT/s, more than doubling DDR5’s baseline transfer rate.

texto_fonte:
Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.
JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.
One of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.
JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.
Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.
DDR6 Specifications
Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.
Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.
DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).
Consumer DDR5 memory modules currently sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.
DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.

texto_fonte:
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.
Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”
Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).
Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.
Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”
In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.
“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”
Milestones, challenges
Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.
“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”
Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.
With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.
As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world.
“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”

texto_fonte:
Behind Equinix and Diraq’s collaboration to bring a silicon spin quantum computer into a commercial data center … and what it actually takes to get there.
Insider Brief
- Equinix and Diraq have installed a silicon spin quantum computer inside an operational commercial data center in Sydney. Equinix supplies the power, cooling, physical security, connectivity and facility operations, and Diraq develops and runs the quantum system.
- Jarrod Nink, Equinix’s Managing Director for Australia, says moving quantum from research to production depends on four things: reliability, integration, operational visibility and scalability, describing the project as a chance to learn how quantum requirements may change as the technology matures.
- Petrina Steele, Equinix’s Global Lead for Emerging Technologies, says every quantum deployment is bespoke, stating the company’s goal as multi-modality quantum computing as a service. Diraq is Equinix’s first silicon spin platform, alongside superconducting, trapped-ion and photonic systems already in its ecosystem.
The recent headlines around Diraq and Equinix’s collaboration have focused on a milestone: a silicon spin quantum computer, installed inside an operational commercial data center in Sydney.
Running alongside the servers, the CPUs and GPUs that already power everyday digital infrastructure, it is a milestone that doesn’t just happen on announcement day. Rather, it is preceded by months of groundwork, from facility assessments and operating agreements to the quiet coordination between two teams who don’t normally speak the same technical language.
That is exactly where a story waits to be told, and it is one that Jarrod Nink, Equinix’s Managing Director for Australia, and Petrina Steele, Equinix’s Global Lead for Emerging Technologies are positioned to tell.
Two Kinds of Expertise, One Deployment
Overseeing Equinix’s business across the company’s 18 data centers in Australia—operations, sales and stakeholder management—puts Nink at a critical intersection where quantum hardware development meets the operational discipline of running facilities enterprises depend on every day. His role in this story is as a local voice who speaks to how Diraq’s system, with Equinix’s support, came together on the ground in Sydney, from installation through to deployment.
Nink describes the collaboration as a pairing of complementary strengths.
“Diraq is responsible for developing and operating the quantum technology itself, while Equinix provides the secure, resilient and highly connected digital infrastructure environment needed to host and support that technology.”
—Jarrod Nink, Equinix
That division shapes everything downstream. Equinix’s role starts with the facility itself—power, cooling, physical security, connectivity and operational support. Diraq brings the quantum computing system, built on its silicon spin qubit technology, and the specialist expertise to operate and scale it. “Together,” Nink says, “we’re exploring what it takes to move quantum computing from the laboratory into a real-world commercial environment.”
Andrew Dzurak, Diraq’s founder and CEO, has framed the same partnership from the other side: as a step toward quantum computers becoming a standard part of data center infrastructure, working alongside—not apart from—the classical and AI systems already in place.
Long before any hardware arrived on-site, Equinix ran a detailed assessment of what the deployment would require. “As with any advanced computing deployment, we conducted a detailed assessment of the infrastructure requirements, including power availability, cooling capacity, space allocation, connectivity, physical security and operational support models,” Nink explains.
The goal wasn’t simply confirming the facility could handle a new kind of workload—it was making sure it could do so without loosening the standards of resilience Equinix customers already expect. “Just as importantly,” Nink adds, “we’re interested in understanding how these requirements may evolve as the technology matures and scales.”
That forward-looking piece is important: this deployment is as much a chance to learn what future systems will demand as it is about supporting this one.
The Pattern Behind Every New Technology
Drawing on his work on the Sydney deployment, Nink observes a familiar pattern. It is one that shows up whenever a new kind of computing moves from research into production and is characterized by four recurring themes: reliability, integration, operational visibility and scalability. “Research environments are designed for experimentation, while commercial environments require predictable, repeatable operations,” says Nink.
New technology needs to connect cleanly into existing applications, cloud environments, networks and data ecosystems. Customers expect the same monitoring, governance and security controls they’d get with any other infrastructure investment.
Scalability closes the loop—in Nink’s view, a technology becomes genuinely useful once it can be deployed and expanded within infrastructure that already exists, rather than requiring something purpose-built around it.That framework helps explain why Diraq’s approach fits naturally into Equinix’s environment. Diraq’s silicon-based approach has been designed with deployment and scale in mind, including how quantum systems can fit within existing data centers and computing infrastructure.
Nink treads carefully as we enter the realm of physics, “We’re not experts in the underlying quantum physics, so I would leave the technical comparison of modalities to Diraq.” But, from an infrastructure standpoint, he points to deployability as the standout quality. “As a data center operator, we’re interested in practical considerations such as footprint, operational requirements, integration and how technology fits within existing digital infrastructure environments,” he says.
There is a clear distinction here: systems built with commercial deployment have a real head start and integrate more naturally into ecosystems that already exist, instead of asking the ecosystem to adapt to them.
A Familiar Playbook, With New Pages
Equinix has recent, hard-won experience bringing demanding new workloads online with GPU clusters and AI infrastructure chief among them. Asked how onboarding a quantum system compares, Nink sees real continuity. “There are certainly similarities,” he says. “The industry has learned a great deal from supporting increasingly dense and specialized AI workloads, particularly around infrastructure readiness, resilience, cooling, connectivity and operational support.”
At the same time, quantum computing is earlier in its commercialization journey, and Nink treats this deployment as a genuine learning opportunity as much as a hosting arrangement. To him, projects like this provide valuable insight into the operational requirements, support models and ecosystem integrations that may be needed as quantum technologies evolve.
That same clarity carries into the day-to-day operating model. Accountability is clearly split: Equinix owns the data center environment—power, cooling, physical security, connectivity, facility operations—while Diraq owns the quantum system and the expertise to run it. Layered across both sides are the tools that keep any advanced deployment running smoothly: remote monitoring, defined operating procedures, and clear paths for addressing anything that needs attention.
Security follows the same logic of rigor applied to something new and remains fundamental to every deployment within an Equinix facility. But, this time around, hosting emerging technology brings its own added focus— protecting intellectual property, managing access controls, keeping governance clearly defined.
Overall, the underlying principles don’t change: strong physical security, controlled access, and operational discipline. What’s new is applying that discipline to a technology still defining its own norms.
Where the Real Work Happens
Ask Nink what stands out most from the ground level, and he doesn’t point to a single dramatic fix—he points to the working sessions. “What stands out most is the collaboration between teams with very different areas of expertise,” he says.
Equinix’s facilities and operations teams are used to supporting sophisticated digital infrastructure; Diraq’s teams work at the leading edge of quantum hardware. Bringing those two vocabularies together, session by session, is where innovation moves from theory into operational reality.
For the people doing that work, the core of the job hasn’t shifted: reliability, resilience, security and operational excellence remain the mandate. But, what has expanded is the range of technologies on-site teams now get to work with. Nink frames it as an opportunity for growth, and one that lets teams deepen their expertise, work across new disciplines and develop a broader understanding of next-generation computing environments.
Adaptability and continuous learning, in his telling, are becoming core skills in their own right as data center infrastructure diversifies.
A Connected Future
Zooming out, we can see that this deployment fits neatly into a strategy Equinix has been building for years: an interconnection-first approach that links the cloud, AI, and classical computing. Equinix believes the future of digital infrastructure will be built on a combination of cloud, AI, classical computing and quantum computing. Instead of operating on isolated islands, Equinix speaks to a vision where quantum systems will connect to applications, data sources, cloud platforms and research ecosystems just like everything else.
It is on this stage that Steele, Nink’s counterpart, widens the lens to what Equinix is seeing as quantum computing steps out of the labs and into real-world infrastructure. Her voice in this collaboration runs in parallel with Nink’s, albeit providing a global perspective in assessing the wider quantum landscape.
There, Steele acknowledges a consistent pattern as the technology expands out of the laboratory arena: it is arriving in many forms at once, and no two deployments look alike.
“Every quantum system brings its own requirements, from power and cooling to footprint, integration and operations,” she says. “Each deployment is bespoke, so we sit down with each provider to understand the nuances together before anything goes into the data center.”
In Sydney, that principle has played out in the joint working sessions Nink describes, where Equinix’s facilities teams and Diraq’s teams worked through the details of the installation side by side. It is within this framework that Nink also recognizes the greater question that looms overhead.
“One of the biggest challenges facing the industry is not simply whether quantum computing can work, but how it can be deployed, connected, managed and accessed within real-world operating environments,” he says.
Steele also points to two priorities that shape how Equinix approaches quantum. The goal is quantum computing as a service (QCaaS), where customers access quantum capability through connected infrastructure they already use instead of owning and operating the hardware themselves. Access across multiple modalities matters just as much.
Diraq is Equinix’s first silicon spin platform, joining the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic modalities already in the Equinix ecosystem. No single qubit approach is likely to suit every workload, so giving customers the choice of approach all from one connected environment is central to Equinix’s proposition.
Equinix recently introduced Fabric One, an intent-based networking service where customers describe the outcome they need and Equinix composes the network to deliver it. It is expected to enter beta later this year, with general availability planned for 2027, initially in North America. The principle of simple, on-demand, any-to-any access across providers suits a multi-modality quantum future, where customers shouldn’t need a bespoke connection for every type of hardware.
“Quantum will only matter to enterprises if they can reach it easily and choose the right technology for the job. Bringing Diraq’s silicon spin platform into Sydney gives us a local foothold in a global ecosystem,” says Steele. “Customers here connect into the same fabric of quantum, AI and cloud that Equinix operates worldwide, and customers worldwide can reach what’s being built here.”
It is an initiative that Equinix and Diraq, through their collaboration, has demonstrated to be viable and important. The project now stands as a concrete step toward proving that quantum hardware can run alongside the AI, cloud and high-performance computing systems enterprises already rely on, inside infrastructure that already exists. Nink sees that proof in the Sydney installation itself, while Steele sees a model for the collaborative approach every future deployment will need, since no two will look alike.

One "day" might not sound like a lot of time or distance, and in the vast emptiness of space, where everything is so far apart, it really isn't. Rather than using familiar measurements such as miles or kilometers, distances in space are often described in terms of how light travels.

Voyager 1 eventually became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space in 2012, with Voyager 2 following suit in 2018. To date, these are the only two spacecraft to have ever achieved this milestone.
To reiterate, both probes have been careening through space since the mid-70s, and only just now has one made it a single light-day from Earth. And to think, some objects in the universe are many billions of light-years away. That truly is absolutely mind-blowing.

candidato.titulo: Google lança Gemini 4 Neon, nova IA para tarefas complexas
candidato.resumo: Modelo substitui Gemini 4 Argon e está disponível para assinantes dos planos AI Pro e Ultra do Google. Google lança Gemini 4 Neon, nova IA para tarefas complexas

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- Google lançou o Gemini 4 Neon, um modelo de IA para programação e análise de dados complexos, que substitui o Gemini 4 Argon e está disponível para assinantes dos planos AI Pro e Ultra do Google.
- O Gemini 4 Neon é projetado para trabalhos que exigem mais tempo e grandes volumes de informação, podendo trabalhar em sessões prolongadas com diversos arquivos e repositórios.
- O modelo está disponível no app do Gemini e pode ser usado por desenvolvedores através da API Gemini pelo AI Studio e no Android Studio, além do Gemini for Business e o Google Antigravity.
Dando sequência a sua série de modelos de IA mais recente, o Google apresentou nesta quinta-feira (19/11) o Gemini 4 Neon. O sistema, quarto lançado na família, substitui o Gemini 4 Argon para tarefas de programação, análise de dados e outros trabalhos corporativos.
Segundo o vice-presidente sênior do Google DeepMind, Koray Kavukcuoglu, o Neon fica entre o Carbon e o Hydrogen, oferecendo mais capacidade para tarefas longas que o último. O modelo também permite ajustar a profundidade do raciocínio do nível baixo ao alto, sendo o alto definido por padrão.
Com a chegada do Neon, o Google aposenta o primeiro modelo da linha lançado há pouco mais de um mês, e segue com três modelos:
- Gemini 4 Carbon: modelo de fronteira para projetos de longa duração e alta complexidade, pesquisa e cibersegurança avançadas.
- Gemini 4 Hydrogen: focado em velocidade e eficiência para tarefas cotidianas.
- Gemini 4 Neon: para fluxos que exigem mais raciocínio, incluindo programação, mas que não seja necessário recorrer ao modelo mais avançado.
O Gemini 4 Neon já está disponível no app do Gemini para os assinantes dos planos AI Pro e AI Ultra do Google. Ele pode ser usado por desenvolvedores através da API Gemini pelo AI Studio e no Android Studio, além do Gemini for Business e o Google Antigravity. Lembrando que o único dos modelos que segue acessível gratuitamente é o Hydrogen.
Gemini 4 Neon atualiza capacidades do Argon
O Neon é um modelo projetado principalmente para trabalhos que exigem mais tempo e que lidam com grandes volumes de informação. Assim como os modelos lançados anteriormente, ele também pode dividir tarefas mais simples para o Gemini 4 Hydrogen no Google Antigravity.
Para pesquisadores, o foco está em tarefas de análise quantitativa, matemática avançada e pesquisa nas quais usar o Carbon seja um exagero. Em cibersegurança, o Google afirma que o Neon pode atuar desde a criação de código seguro até a identificação e correção de vulnerabilidades, usando aproximadamente metade do custo em tokens do Carbon.
Na API, o Gemini 4 custa US$ 3 (cerca de R$ 17) por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ (R$ 90) por milhão de tokens de saída. Entradas armazenadas em cache custam US$ 0,15 por milhão de tokens, uma redução de 95% em relação ao preço convencional de entrada.
IA consegue bons resultados em testes
Apesar de estar abaixo do Carbon na família, o Neon obteve alguns resultados superiores em alguns testes. No Artificial Intelligence Index v5.0.1, que faz uma média da capacidade dos modelos, ele alcançou 61 pontos, contra 60 do Gemini 4 Carbon, 59 do Claude Opus 5.5, da Anthropic, e 57 do GPT-6.2 Sol, da OpenAI.
Outro resultado interessante vem do Agent Arena Index, que avalia agentes em sessões reais de uso. O Neon estreou na segunda posição, com 1.336 pontos. O Google destaca principalmente a capacidade de o modelo mudar a execução quando o usuário corrige uma instrução no meio da tarefa.
Em tarefas de programação, o modelo teve um salto grande na resolução de tarefas sozinho e combinado a outros agentes. No primeiro cenário, no teste SWE-sweep, resolveu 12,8% das tarefas, mas a taxa subiu para 39% quando integrado ao Antigravity.
Ele, assim como o Argon, também se destacou em cibersegurança, com resultados superiores ao Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2 e Opus 5.5. Em avaliações durante a execução de tarefas autônomas, o modelo registrou uma taxa baixa alucinações e alta capacidade de identificar tentativas de injeção de prompt.

candidato.titulo: Harvesting electricity from prickly pear cacti
candidato.resumo: In a greenhouse at the University of California, Santa Cruz, electricity gently hums, but it isn't coming from a lightbulb or socket. Instead, the voltage is being produced from the stems of prickly pear cacti, which researchers converted into living solar panels.

texto_fonte:
Harvesting electricity from prickly pear cacti
In a greenhouse at the University of California, Santa Cruz, electricity gently hums, but it isn't coming from a lightbulb or socket. Instead, the voltage is being produced from the stems of prickly pear cacti, which researchers converted into living solar panels.
A team of scientists developed a technique to harvest small amounts of power from cacti that takes advantage of the plants' specialized, water-preserving approach to photosynthesis. They envision that this green renewable electricity source could power sensors on farms that measure crop conditions amid increasing climate change–related pressures.
A new study published in the journal Plants, People, Planet demonstrates the team's approach to capturing energy from prickly pear cacti and shows how environmental conditions affect cactus voltage strength.
Undergraduate researchers from three academic divisions at UC Santa Cruz contributed to this project, enabling the students to design climate solutions with an approach that felt true to the campus' spirit.
"The undergraduate students told me they liked this project so much because it felt whimsical, and like a lighthearted approach to something that is so serious," said Charlie Chesney, an environmental studies Ph.D. alumna who led the project. "It was a fun way to explore climate solutions that put creativity first."
Electricity from acid
Environmental studies professor Michael Loik, who has been studying cactus physiology and ecology for around 40 years, spearheaded the project with Chesney.
"I've been obsessed with the plant since forever, it seems," Loik said.
To transform cacti into power generators, the researchers take advantage of their specialized method for photosynthesis, called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). Prickly pear cacti and other plants such as aloe, pineapple and dragon fruit use CAM photosynthesis to preserve water for survival in hot, dry conditions.
CAM plants process carbon dioxide into sugar over the course of 24 hours to take advantage of cooler temperatures during the night, while all other plants only photosynthesize while the sun is out.
Other plants open small pores in their leaves during the day to take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) and use sunlight to convert it to sugar—but opening up the pores lets water escape. To preserve precious water, CAM plants only take in CO₂ at night, converting it to a chemical called malic acid.
When the sun comes up and hits the cactus, photosynthesis begins to break down the malic acid, but only on the side of the plant facing the light. That's because CAM plants have thick, opaque stems—another technique to conserve water—which only perform photosynthesis in the outer two millimeters of each side.
This difference in acidity between the sunny and shady sides of the plant causes a pH concentration gradient, which creates a voltage that the researchers harvested.
Turning plants into solar panels
Loik's extensive knowledge of prickly pear cacti led him to predict that electricity production would be possible, but he, Chesney and the team set out to prove and measure it with cacti in plots at the UCSC Farm, greenhouses and laboratories.
Chesney assembled a large team of undergraduate students from the Engineering, Sciences, and Social Sciences divisions at UC Santa Cruz, enabling each student to contribute their knowledge and interests to the project. Now, seven of those former undergraduate researchers are published study authors.
"This was such a cool demonstration of being a really, truly interdisciplinary project, and bringing together so many different undergrads who had different focuses," Chesney said. "It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we're looking at climate solutions, that's what we need."
After years of experimentation, the team found their cactus solar panels could produce a voltage of up to half a volt, which they harvest via a wired electrode inserted into the plant. The team also pursued methods to increase the voltage by adding multiple wires to harvest energy and connecting cactus stems together. By linking together eight cactus stems, they generated a whopping 4.5 volts of electricity—by comparison, a standard AA battery generates 1.5 volts.
Now that Chesney has graduated, electrical and computer engineering assistant professor Colleen Josephson and her Ph.D. student John Madden are carrying forward the project to further enhance the electrical signals produced from the plants.
On-farm energy sources
The team envisions that electricity harvested from the prickly pear cacti could be used to charge low-power agricultural monitoring sensors, which are increasingly in demand due to rising pressures on crops from climate change. By planting prickly pear cacti alongside other crops, farmers would have a renewable power source for sensors to monitor field conditions.
Or, the electricity harvesting could serve to monitor the health of the plant, as the plant is commonly grown for its edible stems (nopales) and fruits (tunas). The timing and magnitude of the voltage, a direct reflection of the cacti's photosynthesis, offer a window into the plant's health and that of the surrounding environment.
"There are many commercial applications of cacti for monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered," Loik said. "This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue. It could be connected to a plant that acts as a sentinel, measuring conditions and sending it back to the base station at the farmer's office."
The researchers hypothesize that their technique could work with other CAM plants like agave or pineapple, although some plants may be more sensitive to the wires needed to harvest electricity.
Impact of environmental factors
The team wanted to investigate the impact of environmental conditions on voltage production for on-farm cactus sensors. They found that the voltage is much higher in the summer when there's lots of sunlight versus during the winter.
"Just how closely the voltage aligned with the sunlight conditions was really surprising," Chesney said. "Comparing winter to summer voltage, the voltage really follows the same pattern of the amount of sunlight throughout the day."
However, too much sunlight can also be a problem.
"If it's too high, then the cactus will start trying to protect itself from sunburn, which will also decrease the voltage," Chesney said. "There's a balance, a midrange of light that causes the voltage to be higher."
They also looked into the effect of drought, a common challenge for cacti. After 15 months without water, not only were the cacti still alive and photosynthesizing, but sometimes the voltage in the drought-stressed stems was actually higher than in the well-watered stems.
"This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it's near death," Chesney said.
Led by undergraduate Erin Langness, the team also investigated the impact of nitrogen, which is a common ingredient in fertilizers because it boosts photosynthesis. Adding nitrogen to the prickly pear cacti boosted the plants' supply of malic acid, which meant photosynthesis and voltage production lasted later into the day.

texto_fonte:
Vulnerabilidade crítica afeta milhões de sites, apps e serviços feitos em Java
Por Marcelo Fischer |
Uma vulnerabilidade crítica no Java pode permitir que criminosos invadam sites, aplicativos e serviços que utilizam a linguagem de programação. Identificada como CVE-2026-114938 e chamada de Java4Shell, a falha permite a execução remota de códigos maliciosos, em alguns casos sem que o invasor precise de login ou senha.
A brecha foi divulgada na terça-feira (17) pela empresa de segurança Calif e recebeu uma pontuação de 9,2 em uma escala de gravidade que vai até 10. A Oracle, responsável pelo Java, já disponibilizou atualizações para corrigir o problema.
Segundo o Tom's Hardware, a exploração pode permitir o acesso a informações confidenciais, incluindo dados de usuários, e abrir caminho para o comprometimento de sistemas inteiros.
O problema está no OpenJDK, implementação de código aberto do Java utilizada como base para diferentes distribuições da linguagem. Como essa tecnologia está presente em sistemas corporativos, servidores e aplicações na internet, a vulnerabilidade tem um alcance potencial elevado.
Como funciona a vulnerabilidade no Java?
A Java4Shell afeta um componente responsável pela decodificação de informações no formato Base64, utilizado para representar dados em texto. Esse recurso aparece em processos de autenticação, envio de arquivos e comunicação entre serviços.
Os pesquisadores descobriram que uma sequência de apenas 64 letras "A", seguida do sinal de igual (=), pode provocar um erro no processamento dos dados em sistemas vulneráveis.
Isso acontece porque uma otimização utilizada para acelerar o processo permite que informações sejam gravadas fora do espaço de memória reservado. Dependendo das condições, um criminoso pode explorar essa falha para acessar dados ou executar comandos no servidor.
A exploração depende de requisitos específicos de hardware e software. A brecha afeta determinados processadores Intel e AMD compatíveis com a tecnologia AVX-512 VBMI, incluindo modelos das famílias Intel Ice Lake e AMD Zen 4.
Sistemas baseados na arquitetura ARM64 não são afetados por essa vulnerabilidade.
Quais serviços estão em risco?
Durante os testes, a Calif conseguiu explorar a falha em diferentes ferramentas utilizadas por empresas e desenvolvedores.
Entre os serviços em que os pesquisadores demonstraram ataques sem autenticação estão Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory e PingFederate.
Também foram realizados testes bem-sucedidos no Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, Apache Solr, Gerrit e Spinnaker, mas, nesses casos, a execução remota de código exigiu autenticação.
Isso não significa que todas as instalações dessas ferramentas estejam vulneráveis. O risco depende da versão do Java, do processador utilizado e da possibilidade de um invasor enviar dados ao componente afetado.
Segundo o alerta do CERT-EU, estão entre as versões vulneráveis o Java 17, a partir da versão 17.0.6, e versões das linhas 21, 25 e 27 anteriores às respectivas correções. Uma edição específica do Java 8 voltada a desempenho também é afetada.
Como se proteger da Java4Shell?
A Oracle publicou correções em 17 de novembro para as principais versões afetadas. Entre as atualizações disponibilizadas estão:
- Java 17.0.21.1;
- Java 21.0.13.1;
- Java 25.0.5.1;
- Java 27.0.1.1.
Empresas e administradores de sistemas devem verificar quais versões do Java estão em uso, inclusive aquelas incluídas diretamente em aplicativos e servidores.
O CERT-EU recomenda priorizar serviços acessíveis pela internet. Quando a atualização imediata não é possível, uma alternativa temporária é desativar a otimização vulnerável com o parâmetro "-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics" na máquina virtual Java.
Até 18 de novembro, empresas de segurança como a Check Point não haviam identificado ataques confirmados explorando a vulnerabilidade em ambientes reais. Entretanto, a Calif já demonstrou a possibilidade de invasão em laboratório e publicou detalhes técnicos sobre o problema.
